prompt: Hypothetical. Five closes are Rs 100, Rs 102, Rs 104, Rs 103 and Rs 105. What is the five-day simple average in rupees?
Why does an indicator built from past closes lag a turn in the price?

options.text: It averages past data, so it reacts only after the price has already moved
It adds information from other markets that arrives late
It is calculated only once a month
It uses tomorrow's close as its input

explanations.b: An indicator adds no outside information. It only uses the price and volume data you already have.
explanations.c: Indicators use daily data in this book. A monthly calculation is not the reason for lag.
explanations.d: No indicator can use tomorrow's close. That value does not exist when the indicator is calculated.

prompt: Hypothetical. A trader sees the short line cross above the long line on a chart. He says this proves the price will rise tomorrow. What is the most accurate response?

options.text: He is right, because a crossover always comes before a rise
The crossing describes past prices. It does not prove tomorrow's move. The rule must be tested before anyone relies on it
He is right only if the long line is above the price
The crossing proves a rise, but only in a rising market

explanations.a: A crossover does not always come before a rise. Crossovers also happen before falls and in sideways markets.
explanations.c: The position of the long line does not turn a crossing into proof of a future move.
explanations.d: The crossing is still only a description of the past. A rising market does not make it a forecast.

prompt: Spot the mistake: "The 20-day average is Rs 248, so the price will close above Rs 248 tomorrow." Which part is wrong?

options.text: The average of Rs 248 itself
The 20-day window
The word "will", which turns a description of the past into a forecast
Nothing. the statement is correct

explanations.a: The average is a correct summary of the last 20 closes. The error is in what the sentence claims about tomorrow.
explanations.b: A 20-day window is a valid setting. It does not change the claim that the average forecasts tomorrow.
explanations.d: The statement is not correct. An average describes past closes. It does not forecast tomorrow's close.

prompt: Which statement is true about two indicators that are both built only from closing prices?

options.text: They are independent, so their agreement is strong evidence
They often agree because they transform the same data, so their agreement adds little new evidence
They always disagree, so one of them must be wrong
They use volume, so they cannot agree with each other

explanations.a: Indicators built from the same closes are related. Their agreement is expected, so it is weak evidence.
explanations.c: Related indicators often agree. Disagreement is normal, and it does not mean one is wrong.
explanations.d: Closing-price indicators do not use volume. Their shared input is the closing price.

prompt: A reader says, "A longer window is always more accurate." Which response is best?

options.text: Correct, because a longer window uses more data
Not correct. A longer window is smoother and slower. It is not more accurate, and the right length must be fixed before testing
Correct, but only for daily charts
Not correct, because a longer window is always less smooth

explanations.a: More data does not make a line a forecast. A longer window gives a slower line that lags more.
explanations.c: The same reasoning applies to every chart period. A longer window is not a measure of accuracy.
explanations.d: A longer window is smoother, not rougher. The claim is wrong because it says accuracy, not smoothness.
